title: What I trust
hookLine: Sariputta's lion's roar of confidence in the Buddha
carry: here is why I trust it

lines: THE BUDDHA DOESN'T JUST ACCEPT IT.
cards: She's the best doctor in the world. This is the greatest band that ever lived. People say things like that out of love, and it's usually more than they could prove.
Sariputta, the disciple known for wisdom, comes to the Buddha at Nalanda and says something like it.
Sir, I'm so confident in you that I believe there has never been, will never be, and is not now anyone who surpasses you in awakening. It's called a lion's roar.
And the Buddha doesn't just smile and accept the compliment.

teach.h: HAVE YOU KNOWN ALL THEIR MINDS?
teach.b: The discourse is the Sampasadaniya, the one that inspires confidence, the twenty-eighth. The Buddha answers with questions. Lofty words, Sariputta.
Have you known the minds of all the Buddhas of the past? No, sir. Of all the Buddhas to come?
No, sir. Of me, right now, so you could say exactly what my virtue and wisdom are? No, sir.
Then why such a bold roar? It's a fair challenge, and Sariputta takes it honestly.

teach.h: NO, SIR. BUT I KNOW THE WAY.
teach.b: He doesn't claim to know what he doesn't. He says: I know it by the way the teaching goes. The Blessed One taught me step by step, each stage finer than the last, and as I understood it, my confidence in the teacher grew.
When the same conversation is told in the account of the last journey, Sariputta adds a picture.

teach.h: ONE GATE, NO GAP FOR A CAT.
teach.b: A king's frontier town has strong walls and only one gate, and a wise gatekeeper walks all the way around and finds no gap, not even one a cat could slip through.
He doesn't need to count every creature; anything large enough to matter comes through the one gate.
So too, every awakened one, past, future and present, passes through the same gate: letting go of the hindrances, establishing mindfulness, developing the factors of awakening.
Back in the Sampasadaniya, he goes on to list, one by one, what he has found well taught.
It changes shape: from I know everything to here is what I've checked, and here is why I trust it. In Pali the word is pasada: a clear, settled confidence, like water after the mud has sunk.

how: Buddhists describe saddha, faith or confidence, as one of the five spiritual faculties, and many teachers explain it as trust that grows through testing the teaching in one's own practice.

o: a formal vow of obedience to a teacher
blind certainty that won't allow any questions
clear, settled confidence, checked for yourself

games.q: what I trust: tap the pairs.
p: made the lion's roar at Nalanda
have you known all their minds?
found no gap for a cat

s: the Buddha simply accepts Sariputta's praise
he asks whether Sariputta has known the minds of all Buddhas, past, future and present.
Sariputta admits he hasn't known those minds
he says he knows by the way the teaching works instead.
the gatekeeper counts every creature that comes in
he knows the walls have no gap, so whatever is large enough comes through the gate.

games.q: you've just told your teacher he's the wisest who ever lived. he asks: have you known the minds of all the wise who came before? what do you say?
o: no, but I know it from how the teaching works, like a gatekeeper who knows his walls.
take the words back and say nothing.
games.why: Sariputta admits what he doesn't know and grounds his confidence in what he has checked.

practice: Name to yourself one thing you trust, a person, a practice, a teaching, a friendship, and ask the Buddha's question: what do I actually know about it? Then ask Sariputta's: what have I checked for myself?
Let the confidence settle like muddy water going clear, and if it's still there, say quietly what you trust and why.

wordCard.voice: pasada. In DN 28 Sariputta's confidence is questioned, and he grounds it in what he has understood of the teaching, like a gatekeeper who knows his walls. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pasada: clarity, serene confidence. the root of sampasadaniya, inspiring confidence.

carryVoice: Your line: here is why I trust it. Settled, like water gone clear. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 47.12 (Nalanda Sutta) and Digha Nikaya 16, parallels with the frontier-town simile
